find: The novel is set against the real Handsworth riots of July 1981 — sparked by aggressive policing, racial discrimination, and mass unemployment in Black communities.
replace: The novel is set against the real Handsworth riots of July 1981 — which followed Brixton and Toxteth, and grew out of racial discrimination, aggressive policing, and mass unemployment in Black communities.
note: F2: the Scarman report called Handsworth 1981 a copycat riot after Brixton and Toxteth; it was not sparked by a local policing operation.

find: Police had conducted aggressive raids on Black-owned businesses and homes. Young people fought back. Cars were burned, shops were looted, and over 100 people were arrested. The riots lasted two days and caused widespread damage.
replace: It began when a well-known police superintendent was attacked as he tried to calm rumours of a National Front march. Young people fought the police. Cars were burned, shops were looted, and 121 people were arrested. The rioting ran from 10 to 12 July and injured 40 police officers.
note: F1: the raids on Black-owned businesses are invented. The 1981 Handsworth riot ran 10-12 July (three days), with 121 arrests and 40 injured officers.

find: data-def="A heavy-handed police operation that used 'stop and search' powers disproportionately against Black people in Britain.">sus laws</dfn>
replace: data-def="An old law that let police arrest a 'suspected person' loitering with intent to commit a crime; it was used disproportionately against Black people.">sus laws</dfn>
note: F3: the sus law was a law (Vagrancy Act 1824), not a police operation. Operation Swamp 81 was the operation.

find: She worked for fifteen years as a <dfn class="term" data-def="A legal professional who represents clients, particularly vulnerable people such as children in care proceedings.">magistrates’ court adviser</dfn> and in criminal law, specialising in cases involving children in care.
replace: She worked for fifteen years in criminal and family law, served as a <dfn class="term" data-def="A volunteer judge who hears cases in a magistrates' court, including family cases about children.">magistrate</dfn>, and sat on adoption panels dealing with children in care.
note: F4: de Waal's own biography says fifteen years in criminal and family law, magistrate, adoption panels. 'Magistrates' court adviser' is wrong, and the definition described a defence lawyer.

find: The dedication reads: “For all the brothers and sisters who were separated.” This signals that the story, while fictional, represents a widespread reality.
replace: The novel is dedicated “For Bethany and Luke”. The story is fictional, but it stands for a widespread reality.
note: F5: the dedication is fabricated. The Penguin edition reads 'For Bethany and Luke'.

expect: Kit de Waal worked for fifteen years as a magistrates' court adviser specialising in cases involving children in _____.
value: Kit de Waal worked for fifteen years in criminal and family law, and sat on adoption panels dealing with children in _____.
note: F4: stem corrected; the answer 'care' is unchanged.

expect: 10-11 July 1981 — after aggressive police raids on Black-owned businesses sparked two days of violence.
value: 10–12 July 1981 — three days of rioting in Birmingham, after Brixton and Toxteth had already erupted.
note: F1: dates, duration and trigger corrected.

expect: Fifteen years as a magistrates' court adviser, specialising in cases involving children in care.
value: Fifteen years in criminal and family law. She was also a magistrate and sat on adoption panels.
note: F4: corrected to de Waal's own account of her career.

expect: 'For all the brothers and sisters who were separated' — signalling the story represents a widespread real pattern.
value: “For Bethany and Luke” — a personal dedication, not a political one.
note: F5: fabricated dedication replaced with the real one.

expect: What is the significance of the novel's dedication?
value: Who is My Name is Leon dedicated to?
note: F5: question matched to the corrected answer.

expect: A heavy-handed police operation that used 'stop and search' powers disproportionately against Black people in Britain.
value: An old law that let police arrest a 'suspected person' loitering with intent to commit a crime; it was used disproportionately against Black people.
note: F3: sus law was a law, not a police operation.
F4: de Waal was a magistrate.

expect: A legal professional who represents clients, particularly vulnerable people such as children in care proceedings.
value: A volunteer judge who hears cases in a magistrates' court, including family cases about children.
note: F4: the old definition described a defence lawyer, not a magistrate.

find: Maureen is a Jamaican-British woman who has fostered many children.
replace: Maureen is a white British woman who has fostered many children.
note: F6: Maureen is Leon's white foster carer. Tufty, the Black gardener at the allotments, is the one who gives Leon a link to his heritage.

find: She represents the <dfn class="term" data-def="A community or cultural group that provides identity, belonging, and support outside of official institutions.">diaspora community</dfn> — people who understand racial identity and cultural belonging in ways the white care system does not.
replace: She cannot give Leon a link to his Black heritage, though. He finds that later, with Tufty and the men at the allotments — the <dfn class="term" data-def="People who live away from the homeland of their family or ancestors and who keep a shared culture and identity.">diaspora</dfn> community the white care system never offers him.
note: F6: Maureen is white; the cultural link comes from Tufty. The old definition of 'diaspora' was also wrong.
F6: term matched to the corrected definition.

expect: A community or cultural group that provides identity, belonging, and support outside of official institutions.
value: People who live away from the homeland of their family or ancestors and who keep a shared culture and identity.
note: F6: 'diaspora' means dispersed people, not any informal support network.

find: Cultural identity: Maureen gives Leon something the system cannot — a connection to his Black heritage. She cooks Caribbean food, uses Jamaican dialect, and normalises his mixed-race identity in ways that no social worker has done.
replace: Cultural identity: Maureen is white, so she cannot give Leon a link to his Black heritage. De Waal makes that gap deliberate. Leon fills it later at the allotments, with Tufty.
note: F6: Maureen does not cook Caribbean food or speak Jamaican dialect; that material is invented.

find: Maureen’s garden becomes a central <dfn class="term" data-def="Something that represents a larger idea or concept beyond its literal meaning in a text.">symbol</dfn> in Part 2. Leon works in the garden, planting seeds and watching things grow.
replace: The allotment where Leon meets Tufty and Mr Devlin becomes a central <dfn class="term" data-def="Something that represents a larger idea or concept beyond its literal meaning in a text.">symbol</dfn>. Leon works there, planting seeds and watching things grow.
note: F7: the gardening happens at a community allotment Leon finds himself, not in a garden belonging to Maureen.

find: Leon is allowed <dfn class="term" data-def="Supervised meetings between a child in care and their birth family, arranged by social services.">contact visits</dfn> with Jake, but these become less frequent over time. Each visit is both joyful and agonising — Leon sees Jake changing, growing, becoming part of another family. The visits are supervised, timed, and controlled by adults. Leon has no power over when he sees his brother or for how long.
replace: Leon is allowed <dfn class="term" data-def="Supervised meetings between a child in care and their birth family, arranged by social services.">contact visits</dfn> with his mother Carol, but Carol often does not come. Contact with Jake stops at the adoption: Leon is promised he will see his brother again, and the promise is not kept. The visits are supervised, timed, and controlled by adults. Leon has no power over when he sees his family or for how long.
note: F8: there are no continuing contact visits with Jake. Contact with Jake ends when he is adopted; the supervised visits are with Carol, who often fails to attend.

find: De Waal uses the diminishing visits structurally: as the gaps between contact grow longer, the reader feels Leon’s grip on his brother loosening.
replace: De Waal uses the missed and dwindling visits structurally: as contact fades, the reader feels Leon’s grip on his family loosening.
note: F8: follows the correction above.

find: Maureen provides love, stability, and cultural identity, but cannot replace Leon’s lost family.
replace: Maureen provides love and stability, but she cannot give Leon his Black heritage or replace his lost family.
note: F6: Maureen is white and cannot supply cultural identity.

find: she provides love and cultural identity, but cannot reunite the brothers
replace: she provides love and safety, but she cannot give Leon his Black heritage and cannot reunite the brothers
note: F6: as above.
F7: the allotment is not Maureen's garden.

expect: Maureen gives Leon a connection to his Black _____ that the white care system cannot provide.
value: Tufty, the gardener Leon meets at the allotments, gives him a connection to his Black _____.
note: F6: the stem attributed Tufty's role to Maureen; the answer 'heritage' is unchanged.

expect: A warm, practical Jamaican-British woman who has fostered many children.
value: A warm, practical white foster carer who has looked after many children.
note: F6: Maureen is white.

expect: A connection to his Black heritage.
value: Everyday love, safety and stability — but not a link to his Black heritage; that comes from Tufty.
note: F6: as above.

expect: How does Maureen normalise Leon's mixed-race identity at home?
value: Who gives Leon a link to his Black heritage?
note: F6: Maureen does not do this.

expect: She cooks Caribbean food and uses Jamaican dialect.
value: Tufty, a Black gardener at the allotments, who becomes a father figure to Leon.
note: F6: as above.

expect: What does Maureen's garden symbolise in My Name is Leon?
value: What does the allotment symbolise in My Name is Leon?
note: F7: the allotment is not Maureen's garden.

expect: What happens to Leon's contact visits with Jake over time?
value: What happens to Leon's contact visits over time?
note: F8: contact with Jake ends at the adoption.

expect: They become less frequent, loosening his grip on his brother.
value: Contact with Jake ends at the adoption, and Carol often fails to come to her supervised visits.
note: F8: as above.

expect: Analyse how De Waal uses the contact visits to show the gradual erosion of Leon and Jake's bond.
value: Analyse how De Waal uses the contact visits to show the gradual erosion of Leon's family bonds.
note: F8: the visits are with Carol, not Jake.

find: Leon is now settled at Maureen’s but consumed by his mission to find Jake.
replace: Maureen is in hospital, so Leon is now living with her sister Sylvia, and he is consumed by his mission to find Jake.
note: F9: by the riot section Maureen has been taken into hospital and Leon has been moved to Sylvia's house.

find: Maureen is Jamaican-British, warm, patient, and experienced. She represents an alternative model of care — community-based, culturally aware, and rooted in love rather than procedure. Her home is sensory: food, music, colour, conversation. She provides Leon with stability, cultural identity, and the first genuine safety he has known.
replace: Maureen is white, warm, patient, and experienced. She represents an alternative model of care — home-based and rooted in love rather than procedure. Her home is sensory: food, warmth, comfort, conversation. She provides Leon with stability and the first genuine safety he has known. What she cannot give him is a link to his Black heritage.
note: F6: Maureen is white; the cultural-identity claim belongs to Tufty.

find: Tina: The Social Worker
replace: Salma: The Social Worker
note: F10: Tina is 'Auntie Tina', Carol's neighbour and friend from chapter 1. Leon's social worker is Salma.

find: Tina represents the institutional system.
replace: Salma, Leon’s social worker, represents the institutional system.
note: F10: as above.

find: De Waal presents Tina with <dfn
replace: De Waal presents Salma with <dfn
note: F10: as above.

find: Tina’s language is significant:
replace: Salma’s language is significant:
note: F10: as above.

find: <dfn class="term" data-def="A simple or one-dimensional character who represents a single quality and does not develop.">naïveté</dfn>
replace: <dfn class="term" data-def="Lack of experience or understanding; innocence about how the adult world works.">naïveté</dfn>
note: F11: the definition given was the definition of a flat character, not of naivety.

find: Tina illustrates how institutional racism operates through well-meaning individuals following flawed systems.
replace: Salma illustrates how institutional racism operates through well-meaning individuals following flawed systems.
note: F10: Tina is not the social worker.

find: De Waal presents Tina without villainy
replace: De Waal presents Salma without villainy
note: F10: as above.

expect: Analyse how De Waal uses Tina to explore institutional failure.
value: Analyse how De Waal uses Salma to explore institutional failure.
note: F10: as above.

expect: Mastering: Analyses Tina as neither villain nor hero — she represents a system that fails through process rather than malice. Discusses bureaucratic language as a form of violence. Links to De Waal’s purpose of showing how institutional racism operates through well-meaning individuals. Secure: Explains Tina’s role as system representative with examples. Developing: Describes Tina’s actions. Emerging: Basic account of what Tina does.
value: Mastering: Analyses Salma as neither villain nor hero — she represents a system that fails through process rather than malice. Discusses bureaucratic language as a form of violence. Links to De Waal’s purpose of showing how institutional racism operates through well-meaning individuals. Secure: Explains Salma’s role as system representative with examples. Developing: Describes Salma’s actions. Emerging: Basic account of what Salma does.
note: F10: as above.

expect: Tina uses _____ and bureaucratic language that obscures what is really happening to Leon.
value: Salma uses _____ and bureaucratic language that obscures what is really happening to Leon.
note: F10: as above.
F10: as above.

value: Everyday love and a stable home
note: F6: Maureen supplies love and stability, not cultural identity.

expect: An alternative model of care — community-based, culturally aware and rooted in love, not procedure.
value: An alternative model of care — steady, home-based and rooted in love rather than procedure.
note: F6: Maureen is white and is not the source of Leon's cultural identity.

expect: How is Tina (the social worker) characterised?
value: How is Salma (the social worker) characterised?
note: F10: as above.

find: Present tense sections: De Waal shifts into present tense at moments of high emotional intensity, creating immediacy and drawing the reader into Leon’s present-moment experience.
replace: Present tense: De Waal writes the whole novel in the present tense, so events feel as though they are happening now, beside Leon.
note: F12: the novel is in the present tense from its first line ('No one has to tell Leon that this is a special moment'); there is no shift.

find: The novel is structured in three distinct parts, each representing a phase of Leon’s experience and a widening of the novel’s scope from domestic to political:
replace: De Waal writes in short, dated chapters rather than named parts. These lessons group them into three phases, each a stage of Leon’s experience and a widening of the novel’s scope from domestic to political:
note: F13: the novel has 42 numbered chapters headed with dates, not three parts. The three phases are a teaching frame.

find: Leon’s race is rarely stated explicitly — it is shown through how others respond to him. Carol’s diagnosis is never named.
replace: Leon names his own colour on the first page, but no one ever explains to him what it will cost him. Carol’s diagnosis is never named.
note: F14: Leon states his race in chapter 1 ('he's dark brown and I'm light brown'), so 'rarely stated explicitly' is wrong.

expect: The novel's three-part structure moves from domestic to institutional to _____.
value: The novel's three phases move from domestic to institutional to _____.
note: F13: the novel is not divided into parts.
F12: there are no shifts; the whole novel is present tense.
F12: as above.

expect: When does De Waal shift into present tense?
value: What tense is the novel written in?
note: F12: as above.

expect: At moments of high emotional intensity — creating immediacy and drawing readers into Leon's now.
value: The present tense, all the way through — events feel as though they are happening now, beside Leon.
note: F12: as above.

expect: Three parts — domestic (Part 1), institutional (Part 2), political (Part 3) — widening scope.
value: Short chapters headed with dates. These lessons group them into three phases: domestic, then institutional, then political.
note: F13: the novel has dated chapters, not parts.

expect: Leon's race, Carol's diagnosis and adults' decisions are never stated directly — the reader infers, mirroring Leon's powerlessness.
value: Carol's diagnosis and the adults' decisions are never stated directly — the reader infers them, mirroring Leon's powerlessness.
note: F14: Leon's race is stated directly in chapter 1.

expect: Analyse how De Waal uses the three-part structure to develop meaning in the novel.
value: Analyse how De Waal uses the novel's structure to develop meaning.
note: F13: the novel is not divided into three parts.

expect: Mastering: Analyses Leon’s sensory/physical language vs. institutional euphemism. Discusses how Maureen’s warm dialect contrasts with Tina’s bureaucratic register. Links language to power, identity, and belonging. Explores how register shifts reveal the care system’s dehumanising processes. Secure: Identifies contrasting registers with examples. Developing: Notes different characters speak differently. Emerging: Basic awareness.
value: Mastering: Analyses Leon’s sensory/physical language vs. institutional euphemism. Discusses how Maureen’s warm, plain speech contrasts with Salma’s bureaucratic register. Links language to power, identity, and belonging. Explores how register shifts reveal the care system’s dehumanising processes. Secure: Identifies contrasting registers with examples. Developing: Notes different characters speak differently. Emerging: Basic awareness.
note: F10: Tina is not the social worker; Maureen has no dialect.

find: De Waal shows racism as structural rather than individual. No single character says anything overtly racist. Instead, racism operates through processes:
replace: De Waal shows racism working in two ways. Some characters are openly racist, and the police harass Black people on the street. But the deeper harm is structural: racism also operates through processes:
note: F15: the novel contains open racism and racial slurs, plus police brutality; 'no single character says anything overtly racist' is false and contradicts this lesson's own later paragraph.

find: Neither social worker is personally racist — but the outcome is racist.
replace: The social workers do not act out of personal hatred — but the outcome is racist.
note: F15: follows the correction above.

find: Maureen provides cultural anchoring that the care system cannot. Through her, Leon gains access to Caribbean food, music, language, and community.
replace: Tufty provides the cultural anchoring that the care system and Leon’s white carers cannot. Through Tufty and the allotment men, Leon gains access to Caribbean food, music, language, and community.
note: F6: Maureen is white; Tufty is the source of Leon's cultural identity.

find: Maureen’s role in the novel is partly a corrective to this — showing what culturally competent care looks like.
replace: Leon is placed with white carers, so De Waal gives him Tufty instead — a Black father figure who supplies what the placement cannot.
note: F6: as above.

expect: As structural, not individual — no character is overtly racist but processes and outcomes reveal a racial hierarchy.
value: Both openly, through racist people and policing, and structurally — processes and outcomes reveal a racial hierarchy.
note: F15: as above.

expect: What role does Maureen play in Leon's identity?
value: What role does Tufty play in Leon's identity?
note: F6: as above.

expect: Mastering: Analyses how no character is overtly racist yet racist outcomes are produced — through adoption priorities, ‘adoptability’ criteria, and institutional blind spots. Links to 1980s context and De Waal’s purpose of exposing systemic failure. Discusses the significance of this being harder to challenge than individual prejudice. Secure: Explains structural racism with examples from the text. Developing: Identifies racism in the novel. Emerging: Basic awareness that the novel is about racism.
value: Mastering: Distinguishes the open racism Leon meets from the racist outcomes the system produces — through adoption priorities, ‘adoptability’ criteria, and institutional blind spots. Links to 1980s context and De Waal’s purpose of exposing systemic failure. Discusses the significance of structural racism being harder to challenge than individual prejudice. Secure: Explains structural racism with examples from the text. Developing: Identifies racism in the novel. Emerging: Basic awareness that the novel is about racism.
note: F15: as above.

expect: Mastering: Analyses Leon’s mixed-race identity in a binary system, his fractured sense of self after separation, and Maureen’s role in cultural anchoring. Discusses the title’s significance as a statement of selfhood. Evaluates whether the system truly has ‘no place’ or simply chooses not to accommodate. Secure: Discusses identity and belonging with evidence. Developing: Agrees without nuance. Emerging: Basic description. SPaG: 4 marks.
value: Mastering: Analyses Leon’s mixed-race identity in a binary system, his fractured sense of self after separation, and Tufty’s role in cultural anchoring. Discusses the title’s significance as a statement of selfhood. Evaluates whether the system truly has ‘no place’ or simply chooses not to accommodate. Secure: Discusses identity and belonging with evidence. Developing: Agrees without nuance. Emerging: Basic description. SPaG: 4 marks.
note: F6: as above.
